units.spoken: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)
Learn from each stretch of play several times, with a cap on how far one update can change the move chances.

sections.section: 1 Why one big step can wreck a good paddle

units.spoken: Section one, Why one big step can wreck a good paddle
One batch, several passes

Picture a paddle that already hits back most balls, then one update changes its chances so much that it starts missing them. A batch is the group of steps one update learns from, and playing one takes a long stretch.
How. Reuse each batch for a few passes, and cap how far each move's chance may move. One pass is one run over the batch. Without the cap, one update can move the chances too far.
When it works, the paddle keeps learning from the same batch pass after pass, and no single update can wreck it.

The running example is Atari Pong, one game in the Atari family of video games. Each player moves a paddle up and down to hit the ball back past the other. The state is the screen, given as a stack of the last few frames so the ball's direction shows. The moves are up, stay and down. The paddle moves once every few frames of the game; one such move is one step. Each step shifts the paddle only a little, so it has to start moving before the ball arrives. The reward is plus one for a point won, minus one for a point lost and zero on every other step. One episode is one full game. A point ends only when a player misses the ball, so most steps of a game pass with nothing won or lost. J is the average points per game, the quantity the policy's weights are moved to raise; it is points won minus points lost.

The agent is the learner that picks the moves. A state is the agent's situation right now; a move, or action, is one choice the agent can make in a state; a reward is the number the world hands back after each move, good or bad. The agent sees a state, makes a move and gets a reward, over and over. An episode is one run from the start until it ends, and a policy is the agent's rule for choosing a move in each state; it may always pick the same move or pick by chance.

Take a look at this figure. The court is the whole running example in one picture: two paddles, three moves, and a point for every ball the other side misses. The state is the screen itself, so the paddle reads where the ball is and where it is heading from the picture, not from a list of numbers. That is why the moves are so few and the timing matters so much: each step shifts the paddle only a little, so it has to start moving before the ball arrives, and one wrong move can lose the point.

Figure 1 shows Atari Pong, the running example for the whole page: two paddles, three moves, and a point for every ball the other side misses. Take the dashed line down the middle: it is the net, splitting the court in two.
A policy network is a network that looks at the state and outputs the chance of each move.
The policy gradient pushes each move the agent played by a score Psi sub t of how well it turned out, up when the score is positive and down when it is negative.
A smaller step for every weight does not fix this, because a smaller step cannot tell how far each move's chance has moved, so it must suit the worst case and wastes most of the batch.

What this figure is teaching is that one update can wreck a good paddle. The bars show the move chances before and after a single too-big update, and the rally marks below them show the cost: the first seven rallies are hits, the last three are misses in a row. Take the up bar: it shrinks from the longest to a sliver in one update, so the paddle barely plays up at all, and the rallies it used to win start slipping past it. The damage is not gradual; it happens in one step.

Figure 2 shows one too-big update. Below the bars, the first seven rally marks are green hits and the last three are red misses, so the paddle misses the last three rallies in a row. Take the up bar: it shrinks from the longest to a sliver in one update.

The return is all the reward still to come, with later rewards counted a little less. A state's value V of s is the return the agent expects from state s. In Pong, a screen with the ball heading past the other paddle has a high value, and one with the ball slipping past this paddle a low one.

On-policy means learning the values of the same policy that is playing. Policy gradients are on-policy, because each push counts a move as often as the current policy plays it, so play by an older or different policy would push by the wrong amounts. The batch in hand was played by the policy as it was before the update.

Theta old is the frozen copy of the weights that played the batch; theta is the copy being updated. Pi sub theta of dot given s means the whole set of move chances on screen s, up, stay and down together, rather than the chance of one move.
1.1 An earlier hard limit and its cost
Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO), an earlier method, keeps each update inside a trust region, a limit on how far the new chances may move from the old ones in one update.
How far the chances move is measured by the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, how different two sets of chances are.

TRPO's limit needs an expensive extra calculation at every update, and it is awkward with networks that share their layers between the policy and other outputs, or that use dropout, switching off units at random while training.
PPO uses only ordinary gradient steps, the same kind that train any network.
Equation 1. TRPO kept each update inside a hard limit, but that limit cost an extra calculation at every update, so PPO needs a cheaper way to keep the paddle near the chances that played the batch.
Take a look at this equation. It holds each update inside a hard limit on how far the chances can move.

The limit line. E hat sub t is the average over the batch. KL is the gap between two chance sets. Pi sub theta old of dot given s sub t is the old chances. Pi sub theta of dot given s sub t is the new chances. Delta is the allowed size of the change. The double bar reads as between, old chances against new ones. At or below means the average never passes Delta. Intuitively, average how far the chances moved and keep it small.
termList: pi sub theta old of dot given s sub t
pi sub theta of dot given s sub t

units.spoken: Intuition. One update must not move the chances far, or a good paddle can be ruined at once. The limit holds the average KL over the batch, and the next card swaps it for a cheaper cap.
Example. Take a screen where the ball is far away and both chance sets assign the same chance: the KL on that screen is zero, so it adds nothing to the average.

Example. Take a screen where the ball is coming in high and the old chances favour up. After one pass the new chances favour up a little more, so the KL on that screen is small and the batch average stays small too. If a later pass pushed up much higher, the KL on that screen would grow and the batch average would grow with it, so the limit would stop the update once the average passed Delta.

Inside the limit, TRPO raises a stand-in objective, the surrogate, that rewards making good moves more likely, weighted by how good they were. That surrogate is the CPI objective, conservative policy iteration, the earlier method behind this push.
The KL-penalty version of PPO swaps the limit for a penalty weight. The weight subtracts a cost that grows with how far the chances moved, instead of a hard limit.

sections.section: 2 Capping how far each move's chance can move

units.spoken: Section two, Capping how far each move's chance can move
The ratio measures the drift
Picture the paddle's chance of up drifting further from the chance it was played with, pass after pass, until the paddle barely plays up at all.
How. The ratio compares the new chance of the move taken with the old chance. The ratio is not held inside a band: it can sit past an edge, and past it the push stops counting.
When it works, one batch can be reused for a few passes, and the paddle stays near the chances that played it.
2.1 Score each move against the usual result

Each move in the batch needs a score of how well it turned out. A move's advantage is how much better it is expected to do than the usual result from that state, the baseline. A hat sub t is an estimate of the advantage of the move at step t, built from real rewards and a guess of the usual result. PPO uses the advantage in place of the score Psi sub t.
That usual result has to be guessed.

A critic guesses each state's value, the return expected from it, through a second network, or a second head on the layers the policy shares. In PPO the critic's guess of a screen's value is the usual result each move is compared with.

The network being trained is the actor, the policy network that picks the action; the critic's guesses are used to score how good it was. Actor-Critic's actor push raises the chances of the moves the critic scored above usual and lowers the chances of the rest.

Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) builds the advantage estimate A hat sub t from the real rewards and the critic's guesses, blending short and long stretches of real reward into one estimate. Lambda sets how quickly the long stretches fade. So in Pong a point won many steps later still raises the scores of the moves that led to it, less the further back they are.
2.2 Compare the chance, cap it, repeat the round
Each update works on a minibatch, a small slice of the batch.

The ratio rho sub t compares the new chance of the move taken with the old chance, and the clip sets two edges with epsilon clip: past an edge the push stops counting, so an update stops rewarding a helpful change once it passes an edge.
Epsilon clip is unrelated to epsilon-greedy exploration on the value-based pages.

What this figure teaches is that one PPO round is a loop, and the cap sits inside the loop. The round starts with the paddle playing a batch, and then it passes over that same batch several times, each pass pushing the chances a little. The cap sits under the passes, because every pass is capped, so the paddle can learn from the same batch again and again without one pass moving it too far. The arrow back to the first box says the round repeats, so each batch feeds the next.
Figure 3 shows one PPO round. The arrow back to the first box says the round repeats, so each batch feeds the next. Take box 3: the cap sits under the passes, because every pass is capped.
1. Workers, copies of the agent each playing its own game, collect a batch with the old policy.
2. The critic scores every move: the critic's guesses and the real rewards are blended into each move's score.
3. Run a few passes of minibatch updates, each on a small slice of the batch, on the clipped objective.
4. The new policy becomes the old one.

Take a look at this figure. The dashed line is the push with no cap, rising forever as the ratio grows, and the solid line is the capped push, which flattens once the ratio passes the edge. Each panel draws one edge of the same rule: the upper panel a move that scored well, above zero, the lower one a move that scored badly, below zero. Past the edge the push stops, so a good move stops being pushed up and a bad move stops being pushed down. That is the whole clip in one picture.
Figure 4 shows one term of the clipped objective against the ratio: a move that scored well, above zero, and one that scored badly, below zero.

sections.section: 3 The clipped push, the critic and the entropy bonus

units.spoken: Section three, The clipped push, the critic and the entropy bonus
Take the smaller of two pushes
Picture a move that scored well, its chance climbing a little on every pass, until it is far more likely than when the batch was played. The push should stop there, not keep climbing.
How. At every step take the smaller of the two pushes: the plain one, score times ratio, and the one held at the edge.
When it works, the push stops at the edge for a good move, while a bad move grown more likely keeps its full penalty.
Equation 2. PPO replaces the hard limit with a cap on each move's chance, so one batch can be reused for a few passes without the paddle swinging far past what the batch supports.
Take a look at this equation. It caps each move's chance, so one batch can be reused for a few passes.

The ratio line. Rho sub t of theta is the ratio for one step. Pi sub theta of a sub t given s sub t is the new chance. Pi sub theta old of a sub t given s sub t is the old chance. Equals means the ratio is the new chance divided by the old. Intuitively, divide the new chance of the move taken by its old chance.
termList: pi sub theta of a sub t given s sub t
pi sub theta old of a sub t given s sub t

units.spoken: Intuition. Each move needs a number saying how far its chance has moved since the batch was played.
Example. Take the first pass for a move that scored well: its new chance is barely above its old one, so the ratio sits near one.

The surrogate line. L C P I of theta is the surrogate objective. E hat sub t is the batch average over the steps. Rho sub t says how much more often the move is played. A hat sub t is the move's score from GAE. The product pairs each move's score with its ratio. Intuitively, average the score times the ratio over the batch.
termList: L C P I of theta

units.spoken: Intuition. The push should reward making good moves more likely, weighted by how good they were.

The clipped ratio line. Rho bar sub t is the clipped ratio, the bar marking the clip. Rho sub t is the ratio the clip holds. Epsilon clip sets the two edges of the band. Clip holds the ratio inside the band, one minus to one plus epsilon clip. Intuitively, the clipped ratio sticks at the edge past it.
Intuition. The ratio must stop counting once it has moved far enough: the cap is a band around one.
Example. Take a ratio past the right edge on a later pass: the clipped ratio sticks at the edge, so the push stops there.

The clipped objective line. L C L I P of theta is the clipped objective. E hat sub t is the batch average over the steps. Rho sub t times A hat sub t is the plain push. Rho bar sub t times A hat sub t is the capped push. Min takes the smaller of the plain term and the capped term. Intuitively, the min picks the smaller push, so a good move stops at the edge while a bad move keeps its penalty.
termList: L C L I P of theta
rho sub t times A hat sub t
rho bar sub t times A hat sub t

units.spoken: Intuition. Of the plain push and the capped push, only the smaller one counts, so the push stops at the edge.
Example. Take a move that scored well after several passes: once the ratio passes the right edge, the push stops.
Entropy, H, is how undecided the policy is; it is high when the moves are about equally likely and zero when one move is certain.
The entropy bonus is a small extra term that rewards the policy for staying undecided between moves, so it keeps trying the others for longer.
Equation 3. The clipped push alone is not a whole training step.
Take a look at this equation. It does three jobs at once: the clipped push, the critic, and staying undecided.

The full objective line. L P P O of theta and phi is the full objective. L C L I P sub t of theta is the clipped push for this step. C sub V is the weight on the critic's fit. V sub phi of s sub t is the critic's guess for this screen. R hat sub t is the target return for this screen. C sub H is the weight on staying undecided. H of pi sub theta is how undecided the policy is. The minus subtracts the critic term, the squared gap between guess and target. The plus adds the entropy bonus, the weight times how undecided the policy is. The square keeps the gap positive, so overshooting and undershooting both cost. Intuitively, one update trains the policy, the critic, and the curiosity together.
termList: L P P O of theta and phi
L C L I P sub t of theta
V sub phi of s sub t

units.spoken: Intuition. One step must do three jobs at once: push the moves, fit the critic, and stay undecided.

Example. Take a screen where the ball is slipping past the paddle: the critic's guess sits too high, so the squared gap pulls it down, the clipped term pushes the good moves up, and the entropy bonus keeps a sliver of chance on the moves the paddle rarely tries, so one update covers the push, the critic and staying undecided together.
So one update does three jobs: it pushes the good moves up to the edge, pulls the critic's guesses toward their targets, and keeps the policy undecided enough to keep exploring.
Section four, Step through one PPO round
The walkthrough runs at the MuJoCo settings, clip 0.2 and 10 passes.

What this figure teaches is one PPO round, pass by pass. The chance bar for one screen shows how likely the move is, and the plot beside it shows the push against the ratio. The dot is the push that counts, and it climbs the clipped line until it reaches the edge. The hollow ghost dot is the push that would count without the cap, and it runs on past the edge, so the gap between the dot and the ghost is the push the clip stopped. The ten pips below are the passes: each filled pip is a pass already run, so by the last stage all ten are filled and the dot stays at the edge while the ghost runs on.

Try it. Step through the walkthrough with the Next button. Watch the dot and the ghost dot: the dot climbs the clipped line and stops at the edge, while the ghost runs on along the dashed line. Read each stage's note as you go: it names the ratio, the advantage, and the push for that pass.

Figure 5 shows one PPO round: the chance bar for one screen, the clipped objective against the ratio, and ten pips, one per pass. The dot moves along the clipped line while a hollow ghost dot runs on along the dashed line, so the gap between them is the push the clip stopped. The two dashed lines are the lower and upper edges; the right edge stops the push for this good move. Take the last stage: the dot stays at the clip edge while the ghost runs on, and all ten pips are filled.

sections.section: 5 PPO's settings and runs with and without the clip

units.spoken: Section five, PPO's settings and runs with and without the clip
Here are the settings for Atari and MuJoCo, and the runs that compare the clip with the penalty.
5.1 The settings differ by test suite
The discount gamma sets how much a reward one step later still counts.
Bias here means the push leans the same wrong way on average, instead of just wobbling from one update to the next; it is not the offset weight inside a network layer.
Counting later points a little less makes the push less noisy, because far-off points hang on many later chance moves and add the most noise; the price is a small bias.
Spread is how much results vary from one training run to the next.
The learning rate eta sets how big a step each update takes.

This table holds the settings for Atari and MuJoCo, and the two columns differ in almost every row. Steps per batch: 128 on Atari, 2048 on MuJoCo, so MuJoCo collects sixteen times as much play per batch. Parallel workers: 8 on Atari, not listed on MuJoCo. Passes: 3 on Atari, 10 on MuJoCo, so MuJoCo reuses each batch far more. Learning rate eta: 2.5 times 10 to the minus 4 on Atari, annealed to zero over training, against 3 times 10 to the minus 4 on MuJoCo. Clip range epsilon clip: 0.1 on Atari, annealed to zero, against 0.2 on MuJoCo, so Atari's clip is the tighter of the two and it anneals away while MuJoCo's stays wider. Critic weight c sub V and entropy weight c sub H: 1 and 0.01 on Atari; on MuJoCo c sub V is not used and c sub H is none. Gamma and lambda: 0.99 and 0.95 on both, the one row where the two columns agree. Gradient-norm clip: 0.5 on Atari, not listed on MuJoCo. Take the clip range and the passes together: MuJoCo trains with a wider clip and many more passes, while Atari uses a tighter clip that shrinks away.

The settings come from the PPO paper: the Atari column is its Table 5 and the MuJoCo column is its Table 3, with the clip range from section 6.2. The gradient-norm clip is the exception: the paper never lists one, and 0.5 is CleanRL's default. Take the clip range: Atari's is the tighter of the two and anneals away, while MuJoCo's stays wider through training.
5.2 Three habits that keep training steady

Normalize the advantages in each minibatch: shift and scale them so each minibatch averages zero with a similar spread, so one batch's pushes do not dwarf another's. CleanRL's Atari script normalizes in every minibatch.
Anneal the learning rate and the clip range on Atari, so large steps early give way to small steps late.

Watch how many moves hit a clip edge in each update, and the KL between the old and new policy: a rising clip count or KL says the policy is drifting too far. CleanRL's Atari script tracks both on every update.
One Atari rollout, one round of collecting a batch, takes 12 gradient steps: 3 passes of 4 minibatches each, over a batch of 8 workers times 128 steps, cut into minibatches of 256.
5.3 The clip wins, and PPO learns fastest

The PPO paper also tried an adaptive penalty weight: halved only when the measured KL sits below the target divided by 1.5, doubled only when it sits above the target times 1.5, unchanged inside the band. The starting weight mattered little, since the rule corrects it fast.

On seven MuJoCo robot tasks, scored so a random policy scores 0 and the best scores 1, and averaged over the last 100 episodes, the clipped version scored 0.82. It beat 0.74 for the best adaptive KL penalty, 0.72 for the best fixed one, and minus 0.39 with neither a clip nor a penalty. The clip won that comparison.
Replay keeps a memory of past steps, and training draws random batches from it.

The paper ran PPO beside two other actor-critic methods, advantage actor-critic (A2C) and actor-critic with experience replay (ACER), an actor-critic that reuses old play by reweighting it with a ratio of new to old chances, much like PPO's ratio, so play by an older policy no longer pushes by the wrong amounts. A2C learns from fresh play by several workers at once, and fits when fresh batches are cheap.

On 49 Atari games PPO won 30 games to ACER's 18 and A2C's 1 when scores were averaged over all of training, so it learned faster; on the last 100 episodes alone ACER won 28 to PPO's 19, so ACER finished ahead and PPO's edge was speed of learning, not the final score.
Section six, PPO training in PyTorch

This is a toy PPO training loop for Pong in PyTorch, to read rather than run; each block's comment names the card line it computes. Its loop follows the structure of the Atari PPO script in CleanRL, a library of short single-file training scripts; the values are the Atari ones from the settings table, and the network uses that script's layer sizes. The loss lines follow the paper's equation 9, not the CleanRL script. Code names map to the cards and the table: N_ENVS, N_STEPS, N_EPOCHS are workers, steps, passes; CLIP_EPS is epsilon clip; LEARNING_RATE is eta; DISCOUNT is gamma; LAMBDA is lambda; GRAD_CAP is the gradient-norm cap. Pong has six buttons; the code keeps the three that move the paddle. The code uses gymnasium, the library that runs the games, and ale_py, the Atari game set it loads. The network outputs three logits, the raw outputs z that the softmax turns into move chances.
This code is a toy PPO training loop for Pong: it plays batches, builds the advantages, and runs the clipped update.

1. Copies of Pong in one batch, each played by the same network for a batch of steps; a finished game restarts at the next step, so every step is a real move. Done marks the step at which a game ended, so nothing after it is counted.

2. GAE: the advantage estimate, built backward from the rewards, the critic's guesses and the done flags. When a game ends, the next guess is dropped, so a game that ended contributes nothing after it. A shifted done index reads the next step's done flag for this step, one step ahead. So the critic's guess is dropped after the move before the game ended, instead of after the move that ended it. CleanRL stores its done flags the other way round, filled before the step runs, so its use of the next step's flag is correct in its own storage.
3. The ratio line of the clip card: the new chance of each move taken, divided by its old chance.

4. The clipped ratio and the clipped objective lines of the clip card: the ratio held between the two edges, and the smaller of the plain and clipped terms, averaged over the minibatch. The minus in front flips the signs, since training minimizes the loss.
5. The full objective card: the critic's loss, the squared gap between its guess and the return it is trained to predict, plus the entropy bonus.

6. Epochs and minibatches: an epoch is one pass over the whole batch. The batch tensors are flattened first, so each minibatch index picks one step; the batch is shuffled and cut into minibatches, and the update runs over each minibatch several times.

sections.section: 7 Where the clip stops the push

units.spoken: Section seven, Where the clip stops the push
Step size and the clip edge

Picture the dot racing along the line toward the clip edge, pass after pass, while the ghost dot runs on past it. The step size is a scaled-up stand-in for the learning rate, how big a step each update takes.

How. Each pass moves the chance by the step size times the push, and the clip stops the push at the edge. The tool runs at the MuJoCo settings, clip 0.2 and ten passes, and varies the step size the walkthrough held fixed.
When it works, even the largest step cannot wreck the paddle, because the push stops at the edge, even though the ratio can still sit past it.

What this figure teaches is where the clip stops the push, and how the step size changes when the dot gets there. The two dashed lines are the lower and upper edges, and the dot climbs the clipped line as the passes run. A larger step reaches the edge in fewer passes, so the dot stops sooner. The open circle on the dashed line marks where the ghost ends after ten passes at the current step size, so it shows the push the clip stopped before any pass runs. Take the largest step size: one pass leaves the ratio past the edge, so the dot sits past it, but the push stops at the edge.

Try it. Drag the step size slider and watch the dot and the ghost. A larger step reaches the clip edge in fewer passes; the largest step leaves the ratio past the edge in one pass, but the push still stops at the edge. Flip the toggle to a move that scored badly and watch the left edge stop the push downward instead.

Figure 6 shows where the clip stops the push. The two dashed lines are the lower and upper edges: the right edge stops the push for a good move, the left edge stops pushing a bad move down. At rest, the open circle on the dashed line marks where the ghost ends after ten passes at the current step size, so dragging the slider moves that circle before any pass runs. Over the passes, larger steps reach the clip edge in fewer passes. Take the largest step size: one pass leaves the ratio past the edge, so the dot sits past it, but the push stops at the edge.

What this figure teaches is the other side of the clip: what happens to a move that scored badly. The solid line is the capped push for a bad move, and it is flat to the left of the clip edge and keeps falling to the right, while the dashed line falls throughout. So making the move less likely keeps pushing it down, but making it more likely stops at the edge: the left edge stops pushing this move down, while the right edge does not stop the penalty. The two dashed lines are the lower and upper edges, and here it is the left edge that does the stopping.

Figure 7 shows the clip tool with the toggle set to a move that scored badly: the solid line is flat to the left of the clip edge and keeps falling to the right, while the dashed line falls throughout. The two dashed lines are the lower and upper edges; the left edge stops pushing this move down.
Section eight, When PPO fits

PPO is a robust default for games, robots and language-model fine-tuning, when fresh batches are cheap enough to collect; the settings still differ by domain, so one set does not work across many tasks.

Prefer deep Q-network (DQN) family methods when steps are costly and replay is needed. When the moves are amounts from a range, such as joint angles or steering, in robot control with few samples, the smooth-moves approach fits.
Section nine, What breaks PPO
Read the symptom, name the fix
Picture a paddle after a long night of training that still loses: its pushes swing wildly from batch to batch, its guesses are wrong, and it has settled on one move too early.
How. Each break has its own cause: the clip range or the passes too large, advantages left unnormalized, a weak critic, the paddle settling too early, and a step that overshoots the edge.
When it works, the paddle keeps learning instead of stalling on one failure, because each break points at its own cause and the fix follows from it.
The clip range or the number of passes is too large: the KL blows up. Lower the clip range or the passes.
The advantages are not normalized: one batch's pushes dwarf another's.
The critic is weak: its guesses are wrong, so A hat sub t is wrong too. Fit the critic.
The paddle settles on one move too soon: raise c sub H.
Clipping does not strictly bound the KL: one large step can still leave the ratio past the edge, though the push stops at the edge. Add an early stop on the KL.
Section ten, PPO for smooth moves

A smooth move is an amount from a range, such as a joint angle or a steering angle, instead of one of three buttons. The policy outputs that amount, and the clip only compares the move's new density, how likely that amount is, with its old one, so the capped step carries over unchanged.
Continuous Actions uses PPO with smooth moves.
Section eleven, PPO for language models
In a language model, each word the model writes is a move, and a reply is a run of moves. The clip still compares the move's new chance with its old one, so the same capped step trains the model.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback uses PPO to fine-tune a language model.
Group relative policy optimization drops the critic and scores each reply against the average result of a group of replies to the same prompt.
